newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK democracy lobby protests China's plans for laws.
newsitem.headline: HK democracy lobby protests China's plans for laws.

text.p: Hundreds of pro-democracy activists marched peacefully in Hong Kong on Sunday to protest Beijing's controversial shadow legislature and its plans to dilute civil liberties when it takes back the colony on July 1.
About 300 people converged on the headquarters of China's de facto diplomatic mission in Hong Kong to deliver a protest petition and a bouquet of flowers labelled: "Human Rights".
"I don't think we are losing the battle...the battle will be lost if we keep silent," Yeung Sam, vice chairman of the Democratic Party which is spearheading the campaign, said.

The colony's governor, Chris Patten, earlier challenged members of Hong Kong's controversial shadow legislature to explain why China needs to scrap civil liberties laws after the handover later this year.
"Many of them actually voted for our Bill of Rights," Patten said in a radio address on Sunday.
The 60-member chamber gathered across the border in Shenzhen on Saturday to avoid legal challenges to its legitimacy in Hong Kong, where opponents have branded it illegal.
The chamber will replace Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council, returned in 1995 under the auspices of Patten's democratic reforms, which were enacted to China's fury.
Its first act was to choose a president, equivilent of a speaker in parliament. Deputies voted for a former colonial official who switched allegiance to China.

Rita Fan, a former Hong Kong legislator and cabinet member and a key player in committees overseeing the handover, was voted president of the 60-member council to be installed upon the handover of the British colony on June 30, 1997.

Patten urged the provisional legislators, almost half of whom sit on the doomed elected legislature to be replaced by the provisional council upon the handover, to explain themselves to the people of Hong Kong.
"I think there's one very simple question which has to be addressed.
"Is Hong Kong going to have the same freedoms after 1997 -- yes or no? If the answer to that question is yes, then why, I repeat, why, do we need to make all these changes?

"And if the answer is no, we are entitled to learn just what is going to be usurped, just how much is going to be taken away, why that's going to happen and how it squares with the international covenants and all the other promises China has made?"
The job of repealing parts of the Bill of Rights and laws on public order and the formation of political parties will be one of the first tasks of the provisional legislature headed by Fan.
China has said the changes will not weaken Hong Kong's civil rights protections after the handover.

The council said it had intended to allow the Hong Kong public to view proceedings, but had to reverse the decision due to a lack of space at the Shenzhen State Guesthouse, a two-storey luxury mansion used by senior Communist Party cadres.
A member of both the existing and Provisional Legislatures admitted regret the meeting had to be held in China.
"Of course, it would be good to have the meeting in Hong Kong. But you don't want to see (provisional) legislators be thrown in jail," member Chim Pui-chun told reporters.
